segments.text: Welcome to the 6th lecture of this MOOC, Introduction to Virus Management.
In this lecture, I will be discussing the World Health Organization Laboratory Biosafety Manual
and the Pathogen Safety Data Sheets.
These are essential guidelines in order to assess the risk posed by known biological agents.
Please note that all risk assessment must be done using known biological agents as a reference.
We cannot conduct a risk assessment for unknown biological agents.
Welcome back to this lecture on risk assessment.
In today's lecture, I will discuss the Pathogen Safety with Data Sheets
as well as specific guidelines in the World Health Organization Laboratory Biosafety Manual
pertaining to risk assessment.
The learning objectives for this lecture are as follows.
I will introduce you to the process of risk assessment for a known biological agent.
Please take note that risk assessment can only be conducted for known biological agents.
We cannot conduct a risk assessment for unknown biological agents
as the risk is not perceptible or the risk is unknown.
We will discuss the key points that must be addressed during risk assessment
pertaining to the characteristics of the pathogen.
And we will also discuss the Pathogen Safety Data Sheets,
which is a very important document that is utilized currently by risk managers across the world.
And we have to be thankful to the Government of Canada for developing this excellent resource.
The learning outcomes for this module are as follows.
Upon completion of this module, I want you to demonstrate the ability to develop a questionnaire
or an instrument for risk assessment, address specific criteria pertaining to risk assessment
based on your own localized situation, and apply the information from the PSDS
to assess the risk posed by a known biological agent.
Risk assessment functions within a scope.
There are risks that are within the scope of an assessment
and risks that are beyond the scope of an assessment.
This is the iceberg analogy in which this is the risk that you see
and which you perceive, and this is the risk which you do not see and cannot perceive.
The World Health Organization Laboratory Biosafety Manual
contains specific guidelines for microbial logical risk assessment.
These focus on specific criteria or characteristics of the microbe,
such as the pathogenicity of the microbe,
the potential outcome of exposure in terms of morbidity and mortality,
the natural route of infection, other routes of infection,
stability of the biological agent in the environment,
concentration and culture volume of the biological agent
with respect to the specific laboratory procedure or laboratory operation,
as well as the presence of a suitable host or vector
for transmission of the biological agent,
the priori information available from researchers
and other studies pertaining to that particular biological agent,
specific laboratory procedures which increase the risk of exposure
such as pipetting, centrifugation and extraction of nucleic acids,
any genetic manipulation of the organism
in case of genetically modified organism
which has been incorporated or endowed with specific traits
such as the increase in host range or the transmission,
local availability of effective prophylaxis or therapeutic interventions
with respect to that particular biological agent.
Please take note that each biological risk assessment
must be conducted for a specific biological agent.
For instance, if you have developed a risk assessment
for mycobacterium tuberculosis,
the same risk assessment cannot be utilized for pseudomonas,
agenosa or coronavirus.
The risk assessment must also take into account
the current availability of facilities
as well as the training elements.
This is a specific questionnaire or an instrument for risk assessment.
Now, the questions have to be very specific
and the answer will be either yes or no.
This is an example which you can adopt or adapt
to your own respective facilities.
The first question is, has the biological agent
been reported to be a pathogen?
In this case, prior information is required, a prior report.
The next question focuses on morbidity.
Does exposure to the biological agent lead to morbidity?
So you have yes or no, as the case may be.
The route of infection, is it via inhalation?
So this may then lead to your risk mitigation strategy,
which involves the usage of respiratory protection
for inhalation such as masks.
Route of infection via contact, yes or no?
Stability in the environment,
is the biological agent viable outside of the host
or does it basically get degraded in the environment,
as in the case of most viruses?
Genetic modifications which may have been carried out
by the researchers and the availability of treatment.
These are the basic questions which you must address
as a virus manager.
We then move on to some of the questions
which you must pose to your laboratory workers
or your principal investigators.
The first question pertains to training.
Has adequate training been provided to the laboratory workers?
If not, additional training must be provided.
So it's either yes or no.
Contingency plans.
These must be put into place in the event of a spill
or in the event of a breach of containment.
The SOPs must be developed.
And if there's a yes, you click on yes.
If there's a no, you just select no.
Facility.
And the facility pertains to the essential equipment,
which is based on the risk group.
One of the essential equipments,
which I've discussed earlier, is the biological safety cabinet.
The availability of the personal protective equipment.
The availability of the waste disposal system
to prevent release of the biological agent
into the environment or breach of the secondary containment.
The security of the facility,
as well as specific SOPs related to managing the pathogen.
As you can see,
most of these questions pertain to processes
within the facility itself and the specific controls.
And one must conduct this kind of a risk assessment
prior to moving on to risk mitigation.
We now move on to the pathogen safety data sheets.
I will be discussing the template itself

as information becomes available.
And as I mentioned earlier,

There are nine sections,
which are described in the template.

into the search engine

it will then direct you to these sections.

So section one focuses on the infectious agent.
The scientific name, the agent type,
whether it's a virus, bacterium, fungus,
or prion is indicated.
The taxonomy is indicated in terms of its nomenclature
and classification.
The synonyms, common names,
the characteristics of the biological agent
in terms of its culture characteristics
as well as requirement for a specific medium.
The brief description of the biological agent itself
and its life cycle.
The properties of the infectious agent,
which relate to its properties outside of the host.
Section two focuses on hazard identification.
In this section,
the pathogenity and toxicity are addressed.
Communicability,
the ability of the biological agent
to be transmitted across the community.
The epidemiology, the host range.
The infectious dose and the incubation period.
The incubation period is the duration
between the exposure to the biological agent
and the manifestation of the symptoms.
Section three focuses on dissemination.
It indicates if a reservoir exists.
The zoonosis and river zoonosis
is the biological agent transmitted via an animal
and specific vectors.
So the reservoir for the biological agent
may be a human host or it may also be an animal host
or an insect.
Section four focuses on the stability
and viability of the biological agent.
As you must be well aware by now,
there are multiple cases of drug resistance
or antibiotic resistance in microbes.
And these have been reported across the world.
And this must be addressed in terms of risk assessment
for stability and viability.
The susceptibility to disinfectants is another issue
which must be addressed as disinfectants
are constantly used in the laboratory
in routine cleanup.
The conditions for physical inactivation,
which may include heat and the application of steam
or ultraviolet radiation,
as well as the ability of the microorganism
to survive outside of the host.
All of these pertain to the stability
and viability of the microorganism
or biological agent.
Section five must address the available
first aid and medical measures,
which include surveillance of the laboratory personnel.
This may be in the terms of a baseline serum study.
First aid and treatment in the event
of breach of containment,
vaccination if it exists,
and profile access of preventive treatment
for the laboratory workers.
Section six focuses on laboratory hazards.
Laboratory hazards are the result of working
with the biological agent.
And these are likely to be LAIs
or laboratory acquired infection
or hospital acquired infections,
as the case may be.
The sources and specimen,
for instance, if a laboratory worker
is working with a tissue sample
or a body fluid derived from a patient
with a known biological agent,
the body fluid may also contain unknown biological agents,
which pose a risk to the laboratory worker.
There are primary hazards associated
with the biological agent itself,
as well as specific hazards which are associated
with operations involving the biological agent.
Section seven focuses on exposure control
and personal protection.
In this case,
we must identify the risk group,
risk group one to four,
the level of containment which is currently available
or which is required,
the PPEs of protective clothing
and other protection which may be required
in the case of a biological agent.
Section eight focuses on handling
and storage of the pathogen,
and this encompasses spills in the laboratory,
which may pose a risk to laboratory personnel.
Appropriate SOPs must be available
to address spills, disposal of the biological agent
after completion of the laboratory processes,
and storage of the biological agent in the laboratory
under the ambient conditions
or the ideal conditions for storage
of that particular biological agent.
Section nine focuses on regulatory
and other information.
